messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Event Recall: Talking about the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
Margaret had spent most of her career as a forensic analyst, methodically examining evidence and reconstructing crimes. But on one fateful evening, she found herself on the receiving end of violence. As she walked home from work, a stranger assaulted her in an alleyway, targeting specific body parts that would later become etched in her memory like scars. In the months following the attack, Margaret began to notice subtle changes in her daily routine. She started to sit with her back against walls, ensuring she had a clear view of the room. It wasn't just about feeling safe; it was about regaining control over her environment. When her husband suggested they try a new restaurant or go for a walk, Margaret would hesitate, citing fatigue or lack of appetite. In reality, she was avoiding situations that might trigger memories of that night. Talking about the future had become particularly daunting for Margaret. Her friends and family would ask about retirement plans or upcoming vacations, but Margaret would grow anxious, feeling like she was tempting fate by making plans. She began to distance herself from social gatherings, fearing that conversations would inevitably turn to her assault. Her husband noticed the change in her demeanor, but Margaret couldn't explain why she felt so lost and miserable all the time. When memories of the event did surface, Margaret's emotions were intense and unpredictable. Sometimes she'd feel numb, as if recounting a stranger's story rather than her own. Other times, rage would overwhelm her, leaving her breathless and shaken. She tried to push these memories away before they fully formed, afraid that confronting them head-on would be too much to handle. Margaret's relationship with food also changed dramatically. She began restricting her diet, often going hours without eating or sticking to bland, unappetizing meals. Exercise, once a source of comfort and relaxation, became another casualty of her trauma. Her husband encouraged her to join him for walks or yoga classes, but Margaret would decline, citing physical limitations that didn't quite add up. As the weeks turned into months, Margaret's avoidance strategies began to take a toll on her daily life. She stopped attending professional conferences, fearing she'd be asked about her work or, worse still, have to relive the trauma in front of colleagues. Her relationships with friends and family suffered as well; they couldn't understand why she was suddenly so withdrawn and isolated. Margaret's sense of inadequacy grew, whispering that she was no longer capable of handling even the smallest challenges. She began to doubt her own competence as a forensic analyst, wondering if she'd ever be able to return to work with confidence. When thoughts about the event did surface, Margaret would quickly push them away, afraid of being consumed by emotions she couldn't handle. One day, while reviewing an old case file, Margaret caught a glimpse of a specific body part – one that her attacker had targeted during the assault. The memory came flooding back, and with it, the familiar rage and numbness. For the first time in months, Margaret felt overwhelmed by her emotions, unable to push them away or distract herself. It was then that she realized she needed help, not just for her own sake but also for those around her who were struggling to understand what she was going through. Margaret made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find a way out of the darkness that had enveloped her life. As she sat in the waiting room, she couldn't shake the feeling that she was taking a risk by seeking help – that somehow, this too would fail her. Yet, for the first time in months, Margaret felt a glimmer of hope: maybe, just maybe, she could learn to face her memories and reclaim her life.
